justice: The street allocates substantial space to multiple users, with broad sidewalks on both sides, a wide carriageway, and planted medians rather than giving all space only to vehicles.
Accessibility appears moderate because the sidewalks look continuous and relatively flat, but no curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossings are visible in this view.

Fairness is supported by the orderly separation between roadway, median planting, and sidewalk edges, yet the image shows no dedicated cycling facility or visible universal-design elements for users with different mobility needs.
safety: A planted central median separates opposing traffic streams, reducing head-on conflict and improving overall road safety.
The roadway is wide, clean, and clearly marked with lane lines, which supports predictable vehicle movement for all road users.
Streetlights are visible along the corridor and the sidewalks are buffered from traffic by curbs and planting strips, but the long straight road may also encourage higher driving speeds.
livability: Continuous street trees and landscaped medians create a calmer residential atmosphere than a fully hardscaped arterial road.
The presence of tall residential buildings directly facing the street suggests the corridor serves everyday living environments rather than only through-traffic.
Livability is limited by the lack of visible active ground-floor uses, seating, public gathering spaces, or frequent pedestrian activity in the scene.
sustainability: The corridor includes extensive greenery in both the central median and roadside planting, which supports shade, air-quality benefits, and urban ecological value.
Street trees and planted strips indicate investment in green infrastructure rather than a fully paved road section.
Sustainability is weakened by the dominance of wide motor-vehicle lanes and the absence of visible bus priority, bike lanes, or other clearly identifiable low-carbon transport facilities.
aesthetics: The streetscape has strong visual order, with aligned streetlights, consistent lane markings, and a symmetrical boulevard layout.
Tree-lined medians and roadside greenery soften the large road surface and improve the visual quality of the corridor.
The tall residential towers appear modern and well maintained, contributing to a neat and coherent urban image.
comfort: Physical comfort is supported by smooth asphalt, orderly curbs, and sidewalks that appear wide and unobstructed.
Thermal comfort is moderate because there are many trees along the edges, but the carriageway and parts of the sidewalks still appear exposed with limited dense canopy cover.
Psychological comfort benefits from the clean, uncluttered environment and separation between traffic directions, though the broad roadway may feel somewhat vehicle-dominated for non-drivers.
walkability: Sidewalks are present on both sides and appear continuous, which supports basic pedestrian movement along the corridor.
Walkability is reduced because no marked crosswalks, pedestrian refuge details, or intersection crossing aids are visible in this image.
The long blocks, wide roadway, and lack of visible active frontage or pedestrian-oriented amenities such as benches make the street less inviting for walking despite its orderly design.
